summary:
Kazakhstan decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 1997, when Article 104 of the Penal Code was repealed and a common age of consent of 16 introduced; lesbianism was never a criminal offence. No statute restricts changing clothes according to gender presentation, and no bathroom or facilities restriction applies.

On 30 December 2025 President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a law banning 'information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation' in public spaces and media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine. The Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025. Kazakhstan now sits alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting 'LGBTQ propaganda' by law. A visitor should treat this statute as in force.

Trans people may change legal gender on identity documents, a right available since 2003, but only after a diagnosis of 'gender identity disorder' involving medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission. Applicants must pay around ₸100,000 tenge. Although since 2023 commissions can in principle be assembled in every region, in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months to start medical transition, and since 2011 document changes require gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation. People under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all.

Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. As of 2020 same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, and in February 2024 President Tokayev signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples. Deputy Minister of Education Natalya Jumadildaeva stated that a parent's sexual orientation would play a 'key role' in approval, assessed through a 'special psychological test'. Critics, including independent media, noted the law was modelled on Russian legislation.

No laws exist protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit. A 2015-16 Pew survey found 89% of people opposed same-sex marriage.

Police conduct toward trans people is described as unhelpful rather than predatory, with no recorded pattern of police targeting. Documentation of bias violence is weak: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE/ODIHR since the 2018 report and has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, an institutional gap that OSCE/ODIHR says would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures.

ILGA-Europe's Annual Review for January to December 2023 documents access-to-services bias, including an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus, and bias-motivated violence in which an LGBTQI activist was almost run over with no investigation. The same review records a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

The Supreme Court upheld privacy rights in a 24 September 2019 ruling, ordering compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, rejecting a 'moral foundations' defence. The women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

ECOM, which has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017, identifies health-right barriers in Kazakhstan alongside informal behavioural practices that policy analysis misses.
tangentialFactors:
A propaganda ban was under active consideration before it was enacted: in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information confirmed it was reviewing the petition 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!', filed by the Union of Parents, which met the threshold for government consideration. Human Rights Watch warned on 10 July 2024 that the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide. The statute signed on 30 December 2025 follows that trajectory.

The 2024 adoption law was modelled on Russian legislation, according to critics including independent media, placing Kazakhstan in a regional pattern of restriction. The 89% opposition figure in the 2015-16 Pew survey indicates the social climate a visitor may encounter alongside the statutory position.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether the 30 December 2025 propaganda statute carries additional penalties beyond the 10-day arrest and fine, or which authorities enforce it in practice. Enforcement patterns against trans visitors specifically are not sourced.

Whether the Almaty medical commission remains the only functioning one after the 2023 regional expansion provision is not confirmed beyond the Wikipedia country coverage cited. The 2015-16 Pew survey predates the current legal regime and may not reflect present-day opinion.
